ICA-001.q: Match each COSO 2013 Control Environment principle with its content:
ICA-001.e: The control environment is the foundation for the other four components.
p: Commitment to integrity and ethical values
Board independence and oversight of internal control
Structures, reporting lines, authorities and responsibilities
ICA-001.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 – Control environment (ICR-114).
Analysis: P1 – integrity and ethical values; P2 – an independent board overseeing IC; P3 – structure, authority and responsibility; P4 – commitment to competence; P5 – enforcing accountability. The control environment is the foundation: if weak, the other components are easily undermined (ICR-013).

ICA-002.q: The CEO of a distributor routinely asks accounting to 'adjust to hit quarterly KPIs', and staff hesitate to speak up. This deficiency mainly relates to:
ICA-002.e: Leadership tolerating window-dressing breaks the ethical foundation; other controls are easily overridden.
o: Principle 1 – integrity and ethical values (tone at the top)
ICA-002.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P1 (tone at the top).
Analysis: The CEO asking to 'adjust to hit KPIs' while staff fear speaking up → leadership tolerating window-dressing and a culture of silence → a foundational integrity deficiency. Detailed controls (approvals, reconciliations) are then easily overridden by management itself (VSA-052).
Distractors: B, C and D are consequences, not the root cause.

ICA-003.q: Select ALL evidence that the Board/Audit Committee meets Principle 2 well:
ICA-003.e: Dual roles and self-approval of related-party deals weaken independent oversight.
o: Regular private sessions with internal and external auditors without management
Approval of a risk-based internal audit plan
The chair is also CEO and self-approves related-party transactions
ICA-003.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P2; Decree 05/2019/ND-CP.
Analysis: Evidence of a well-functioning P2: (A) independent members with financial expertise; (B) regular private sessions with internal and external auditors without management – for candid information; (C) approving a risk-based IA plan (ICR-059).
Distractors: (D) A chair who is also CEO and self-approves related-party deals weakens independent oversight.

ICA-004.q: Under COSO 2013, internal control is effective only if all 17 principles are present and functioning and the 5 components operate together.
ICA-004.e: True. This is the condition for concluding internal control is effective.
ICA-004.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (ICR-008).
Analysis: True. IC is effective when each component and relevant principle is present and functioning, and the five components operate together in an integrated way. A major deficiency in any principle prevents concluding the system is effective (ICR-015).

ICA-005.q: A construction company lets the site manager select subcontractors, approve quantities and confirm payments. Which COSO principle is most clearly breached?
ICA-005.e: One person selecting, certifying and confirming payment is a flawed authority design, with high risk of contractor collusion.
o: Principle 3 – authorities and responsibilities (with segregation of duties under P10)
ICA-005.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P3, P10 (ICR-084).
Analysis: The site manager chooses subcontractors, approves quantities and certifies payment – authority concentrated in one person, with no split between approval, execution and certification → collusion, fictitious acceptance and inflated quantities. The root is a flawed delegation of authority (P3), showing up as missing segregation (P10).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main issue.

ICA-006.q: A hotel chain's newly hired chief accountant has never worked with IFRS while the group prepares IFRS FS. The deficiency relates to:
ICA-006.e: P4 requires attracting, developing and retaining competent people aligned to objectives, including succession.
ICA-006.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P4.
Analysis: P4 requires attracting, developing and retaining competent people aligned with objectives, including succession plans. Preparing IFRS FS with a chief accountant lacking IFRS experience → a competence gap → material misstatement risk on conversion. Remedies: training, hiring experts, conversion advisers.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't directly relevant.

ICA-007.q: A bonus scheme 100% based on sales, with no collection or compliance targets, is a risk factor under Principle 5 (accountability, pressures and incentives).
ICA-007.e: True. P5 requires considering excessive pressure from targets and reward schemes.
ICA-007.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P5.
Analysis: True. P5 requires considering excessive pressure from targets and incentives. Bonuses 100% on sales with no collection or compliance targets → incentives to sell on credit to risky customers and book revenue early or falsely (the fraud triangle's pressure). Balance it: tie bonuses to cash collected, bad-debt and return rates.

ICA-008.q: Select ALL tools that put Principle 1 into practice:
ICA-008.e: Exemptions for senior management undermine integrity and the tone at the top.
o: Code of conduct with annual sign-off
Exempting senior management from the code
ICA-008.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P1 (ICR-175).
Analysis: Tools implementing P1: (A) a code of conduct acknowledged annually; (B) conflict-of-interest policies and declarations (ICR-102); (C) consistent discipline, including managers; (D) a protected whistleblowing channel (ICR-101).
Distractors: (E) Exempting senior managers breaks the tone at the top – signalling 'rules are for juniors'.

ICA-009.q: The internal audit function of a listed company reports both functionally and administratively to the CFO. The biggest risk is:
ICA-009.e: Under IIA standards, internal audit should report functionally to the Board/Audit Committee.
o: Impaired independence – IA struggles to report objectively on areas the CFO controls
ICA-009.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (Principle 7 – independent positioning); Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (ICR-034).
Analysis: IA reporting both administratively and functionally to the CFO → hard to audit the CFO's areas (accounting, treasury, tax) objectively; the CFO may limit scope or edit reports → impaired independence. Standard practice: functional reporting to the board/audit committee.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main risk.

ICA-010.q: Arrange the risk assessment steps under COSO:
ICA-010.e: Without clear objectives, risks cannot be identified.
o: Determine risk responses and control activities
ICA-010.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P6–9 (ICR-115).
Analysis: Order: set clear objectives (P6) → identify risks to them (P7) → analyse likelihood and impact → consider fraud risk (P8) → decide responses and control activities (leading to P10). Without clear objectives, risks can't be identified.

ICA-011.q: A 5×5 risk matrix (score = likelihood × impact). The risk of a key supplier going bankrupt has likelihood 3 and impact 5. What is the risk score?
ICA-011.e: 3 × 5 = 15 → usually high risk needing a response (supplier diversification, safety stock).
ICA-011.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; ISO 31000:2018 (ICR-022).
Working: Risk score = 3 × 5 = 15/25 → high-risk zone.
Note: Responses: diversify suppliers, hold safety stock, track the supplier's financial KRIs (leverage, late deliveries), contingency contract terms.

ICA-012.q: Match each risk response with an example:
ICA-012.e: Responses are chosen on cost–benefit and risk appetite.
p: Stop exporting to a sanctioned market
Install automatic fire suppression in the warehouse
Accept small shrinkage within risk appetite
ICA-012.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (ICR-019, ICR-020).
Analysis: Avoid – stop exporting to an embargoed market (exiting the risky activity); reduce – automatic fire suppression in the warehouse; transfer (share) – insurance, FX hedging; accept – minor losses within risk appetite. Choose by cost-benefit and risk appetite.

ICA-013.q: Under COSO, which types of fraud does Principle 8 require considering?
ICA-013.e: P8 also requires considering incentives/pressures, opportunities and attitudes/rationalisation.
o: Fraudulent reporting, misappropriation, corruption and management override
ICA-013.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P8 (ICR-005).
Analysis: P8 requires considering fraudulent reporting, asset misappropriation, corruption and management override, while assessing incentives/pressures, opportunities and attitudes/rationalisations (the fraud triangle – ICR-061).
Distractors: B, C and D omit other fraud types, notably management fraud.

ICA-014.q: Select ALL significant changes requiring reassessment under Principle 9:
ICA-014.e: P9: identify and assess changes that could significantly affect internal control.
o: Acquiring a company in a new market
Changing the CEO and chief accountant
Changing the logo colour on business cards
ICA-014.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P9.
Analysis: Significant changes needing reassessment: (A) a new ERP – processes, access rights, data migration; (B) buying a company in a new market – different law, culture, controls; (C) a new CEO or chief accountant – lost knowledge, changed tone; (D) unusually fast growth – controls lag, possibly a fraud signal.
Distractors: (E) A logo colour change doesn't affect IC.

ICA-015.q: Inherent risk is risk before considering controls; residual risk is risk after responses and controls.
ICA-015.e: True. Residual risk must sit within risk appetite.
ICA-015.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (ICR-021).
Analysis: True. Inherent risk is before controls and management responses; residual risk is after them. Residual risk must sit within risk appetite; otherwise add responses or revisit strategy.

ICA-016.q: A pharma company sets the objective 'strong growth'. Under P6 this objective falls short because:
ICA-016.e: Good objectives are specific (e.g., +15% revenue, returns < 1%) to anchor risk assessment.
o: It lacks specificity, measurability and tolerances needed to identify risks
It is not in the charter
It hasn't been approved by the tax authority
ICA-016.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P6 (sufficiently clear objectives).
Analysis: 'Strong growth' isn't specific, measurable or bounded by tolerances → it can't anchor risk identification and assessment. Good objectives: revenue +15%, returns < 1%, 100% GMP compliance – from which obstacles and tolerances follow.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't P6 requirements.

ICA-017.q: Consider these statements on risk appetite:
ICA-017.e: No business operates at zero risk; controls have costs.
o: Risk appetite is approved by the Board and aligned to strategy.
Tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective.
Zero risk appetite is a realistic goal for every business.
Risk appetite must be communicated to management levels.
ICA-017.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (ICR-018).
Analysis: True: risk appetite is board-approved and strategy-aligned; tolerance is acceptable variation around specific objectives; appetite must cascade to guide daily decisions. False: zero risk appetite is unrealistic – all value creation involves risk and controls cost money.

ICA-018.q: A logistics company depends on transport software from a small vendor. The risk to identify under P7 is:
ICA-018.e: Responses: source-code escrow, SLAs, contingency plans.
o: Business interruption and third-party dependency risk
ICA-018.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P7; IIA Third-Party Topical Requirement (ICR-106).
Analysis: Reliance on a small vendor's transport software → business interruption risk (vendor failure, end of support, outages) and third-party dependency. Responses: source code escrow, SLAs, independent data backups, continuity plans (RTO/RPO – ICR-105).
Distractors: B, C and D don't fit the case.

ICA-019.q: Match each control type with an example:
ICA-019.e: Combining control types creates effective layered defence.
p: Approving purchase orders before placing them
ERP blocks invoices beyond tolerance vs the PO
ICA-019.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10 (ICR-011, ICR-012).
Analysis: Preventive – approving POs before ordering; detective – monthly bank reconciliation; manual – the chief accountant signing payment vouchers; automated – the ERP blocking invoices beyond PO tolerance. Layering types means if one is bypassed, another remains.

ICA-020.q: A warehouse clerk holds goods, keeps the stock records and performs counts. Which function should be separated first?
ICA-020.e: Separate authorisation, execution, recording and custody; independent counts are a key detective control.
o: Counts must be performed or supervised by someone independent of the storekeeper
ICA-020.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10 (ICR-084, ICR-088).
Analysis: A storekeeper holding stock, keeping the stock ledger and counting it can steal and 'count to match' the edited ledger. First separate the count – the key detective control – to an independent person or supervisor (blind counts – ICR-088).
Distractors: B, C and D don't resolve the custody–recording–checking conflict.

ICA-021.q: When a small business lacks staff to segregate duties, it can compensate with controls such as the owner reviewing bank statements and exception reports.
ICA-021.e: True. Compensating controls reduce risk when segregation is incomplete.
ICA-021.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10 (ICR-148, ICR-170).
Analysis: True. Small firms lacking staff for segregation can use compensating controls: the director/owner directly receives and reviews original bank statements and exception reports and approves large payments – reducing, though not eliminating, risk.

ICA-022.e: IT general controls: infrastructure, security access, technology acquisition, development and maintenance.
o: Selecting and developing general controls over technology to support objectives
ICA-022.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11 (ICR-006, ICR-073).
Analysis: P11 requires selecting and developing general controls over technology: infrastructure; security access management; acquisition, development and maintenance – the foundation making automated application controls reliable (ICR-012).
Distractors: B, C and D are sourcing choices, not control requirements.

ICA-023.q: Under Principle 12, an effective control policy needs:
ICA-023.e: Policies matter only when deployed into procedures and actually performed.
ICA-023.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P12.
Analysis: Effective policies need: (A) clear responsibility for performing and owning them; (B) timely performance by competent staff; (C) corrective action on exceptions; (D) periodic review.
Distractors: (E) Issuing documents without implementation and follow-up is 'paper control' – not operating.

ICA-024.q: The control 'chief accountant reviews the monthly aged receivables report' is more effective if it adds:
ICA-024.e: Review controls need precise criteria, thresholds and evidence of follow-up to be testable.
o: Specific investigation thresholds (e.g., overdue > 90 days, > VND 100m), evidence of review and follow-up
ICA-024.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P12; VSA 330 (management review controls).
Analysis: Review controls are effective and testable only with specific criteria and thresholds (> 90 days, > 100 million), enough precision to catch errors, evidence of review (notes, queries) and follow-up of exceptions to closure.
Distractors: B is form only; C lowers frequency; D lowers the reviewer's competence.

ICA-025.q: Preventive controls are always better than detective controls, so a business needs only preventive controls.
ICA-025.e: False. Preventive controls can be bypassed; detective controls are the second line of protection.
ICA-025.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: False. Preventive controls can be bypassed (collusion, override, error), and overly tight ones slow operations and cost money. Detective controls (reconciliations, exception reviews, counts) are the second line of defence; good systems balance both (ICR-011).

ICA-026.e: It ensures payment only for goods actually received at the approved quantity and price.
o: Purchase order – goods received note – supplier invoice
ICA-026.x:
Basis: Purchase-to-pay control practice (ICR-083).
Analysis: Three-way match: approved PO (quantity, price) – goods received note (actual receipt) – supplier invoice (amount billed). Pay only when they agree within tolerance.
Distractors: B, C and D lack evidence of actual receipt.

ICA-027.q: Under Principle 13, quality information must be:
ICA-027.e: Information overload impairs decisions; quality matters more than quantity.
ICA-027.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P13 (ICR-173).
Analysis: Quality information is: (A) accurate and complete; (B) timely; (C) verifiable and traceable to source; (D) protected with access controls.
Distractors: (E) Information overload impairs decisions; quality and relevance beat volume.

ICA-028.q: A retail chain's monthly management report comes from manually compiled Excel, not reconciled to the ERP. The deficiency relates to:
ICA-028.e: End-user computing spreadsheets need controls: locked formulas, source reconciliation, version control.
ICA-028.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P13 (IPE, end-user computing).
Analysis: Management reports compiled manually in Excel without reconciliation to the ERP → formula errors, missing data, untraceable manual edits → unreliable decision information. Spreadsheet (EUC) controls: locked formulas, totals reconciled to source, version control, independent review.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the nature of the deficiency.

ICA-029.q: Principle 14 includes separate channels (such as a hotline) for staff to report breaches when normal channels are ineffective.
ICA-029.e: True. Anonymous whistleblowing is part of internal communication under COSO.
ICA-029.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P14 (ICR-016, ICR-101).
Analysis: True. P14 includes separate channels (hotlines, independent email, third-party providers) for staff to report violations anonymously when normal channels (line managers) fail or the manager is the wrongdoer.

ICA-030.q: Which example belongs to Principle 15 – external communication?
ICA-030.e: Information from outside parties (customers, suppliers, regulators) can reveal control deficiencies.
o: Receiving and handling customer/supplier complaints about bribe requests
ICA-030.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P15 (ICR-016).
Analysis: P15 covers communication with outsiders, including input from customers, suppliers and regulators (e.g., complaints of staff demanding bribes) – an important source for spotting deficiencies and fraud.
Distractors: B and C are internal communication (P14); D is an IT control (P11).

ICA-031.q: Select ALL information management should communicate to the Board/Audit Committee:
ICA-031.e: The Board needs information to perform oversight.
ICA-031.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P14; VSA 260, VSA 265.
Analysis: Management should tell the board/audit committee about: (A) significant IC deficiencies; (B) fraud involving management; (C) significant accounting policy changes; (D) key risk assessment results – enabling oversight (P2).
Distractors: (E) Staff leave rosters are operational, not board-level.

ICA-032.q: A customer master data report shows 300 customers without tax codes and 50 sharing addresses. This is an issue of:
ICA-032.e: Master data creation/changes need controls: access rights, approval, verification.
o: Source data quality (P13) – risk of fictitious customers, wrong invoices
ICA-032.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P13; master data management practice (ICR-143).
Analysis: 300 customers without tax codes and 50 sharing addresses → poor source data: risk of fictitious customers (fake revenue), wrong e-invoices, lost receivables. Controls: restricted create/edit rights, approvals, tax-code verification on the tax portal, periodic duplicate reviews.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the core issue.

ICA-033.q: Distinguish ongoing and separate evaluations under Principle 16:
ICA-033.e: The scope and frequency of separate evaluations depend on risk and the effectiveness of ongoing evaluations.
o: Ongoing evaluations are built into business processes (e.g., daily exception dashboards); separate evaluations are periodic, such as internal audit
Ongoing are done only by external auditors
ICA-033.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P16 (ICR-159).
Analysis: Ongoing evaluations are built into business processes and run routinely (daily exception dashboards, automated reconciliations); separate evaluations are periodic (internal audit, control self-assessment). The scope and frequency of separate evaluations depend on risk and the effectiveness of ongoing ones.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

ICA-034.q: Under Principle 17, control deficiencies must be reported promptly to those responsible for corrective action, and major deficiencies to senior management and the Board.
ICA-034.e: True. P17 also requires monitoring remediation.
ICA-034.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P17 (ICR-015).
Analysis: True. IC deficiencies must be evaluated and reported promptly to those responsible for fixing them; serious ones to senior management and the board. P17 also requires tracking remediation to completion (ICA-036).

ICA-035.q: Match each line (IIA Three Lines Model) with its actors:
ICA-035.e: External auditors and regulators are external assurance providers.
p: Business and operations units that own risk
ICA-035.x:
Basis: IIA Three Lines Model 2020 (ICR-031).
Analysis: First line – business and operations owning risk; second line – risk management, legal and compliance; third line – independent internal audit; overall oversight – the board/audit committee. External auditors and regulators provide outside assurance (ICR-168).

ICA-036.q: Last year's internal audit finding on ERP access was 'resolved' per IT, yet 15 accounting users can still create vendors this year. The monitoring lesson is:
ICA-036.e: Remediation tracking needs independent validation evidence.
o: Remediation effectiveness must be validated, not just self-reported
ICA-036.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P17; IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 15.2 – monitoring action plans).
Analysis: IT reported 'fixed' yet 15 accounting users can still create vendors (an SoD conflict – ICR-132) → self-reporting isn't reliable. IA must validate with independent evidence (a system extract of access rights) before closing the finding.
Distractors: B, C and D ignore the remaining risk.

ICA-037.q: Select ALL examples of ongoing evaluations:
ICA-037.e: Periodic internal audits are separate evaluations.
o: Automated daily alerts for transactions over limits
Weekly exception report review by the department head
Daily tracking of a returns-rate KPI
ICA-037.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P16 (ICA-033).
Analysis: Ongoing evaluations: (A) automated daily alerts on over-limit transactions; (B) weekly exception reviews by department heads; (C) daily tracking of return-rate KPIs – embedded in operations.
Distractors: (D) An annual internal audit is a separate evaluation.

ICA-038.q: Control self-assessment (CSA) can fully replace independent internal audit.
ICA-038.e: False. CSA raises awareness and early detection but lacks independence.
ICA-038.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P16; IIA (ICR-097).
Analysis: False. CSA raises process owners' awareness and catches issues early, but being self-assessment it lacks independence and may be optimistic. Independent internal audit is still needed to assure the board; it can use and validate CSA results.

ICA-039.e: ITGCs are the foundation for relying on automated application controls.
o: Access management, program change management, computer operations (backup, incident handling), system development
ICA-039.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11; VSA 315 (ICR-073).
Analysis: ITGC covers: access to programs and data; program change management; computer operations (backup, incident handling, job scheduling); system development and implementation – the basis for relying on automated application controls (ICA-040).
Distractors: B and D are application/business controls; C is a purchasing control.

ICA-040.q: If change-management ITGCs are ineffective, the auditor cannot readily rely on a test of one for automated application controls.
ICA-040.e: True. There's no assurance the automated logic wasn't changed during the period.
ICA-040.x:
Basis: VSA 315; VSA 330 (ICR-012).
Analysis: True. A 'test of one' for automated controls assumes logic didn't change during the period – valid only with effective change-management ITGC. If program changes aren't controlled, logic may have been altered mid-year → auditors must test more points in time, do substantive work, or not rely on the control.

ICA-041.q: Developers at a software company can push code directly to the accounting system's production environment. The key risk:
ICA-041.e: Separate dev–test–production environments and restrict migration rights.
o: Unauthorised changes to logic or data without testing and approval
ICA-041.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (8.31, 8.32 – ICR-075).
Analysis: Developers promoting code to production themselves → unauthorised changes to calculation logic (e.g., rounding, allocation) or data without testing, approval or a trail – both error and fraud risk. Separate development, test and production with an independent person deploying (ICA-048).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main risk.

ICA-042.e: Shared accounts destroy accountability and traceability.
o: Periodic access reviews by process owners
One shared account for the whole accounting team
ICA-042.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (ICR-074, ICR-081, ICR-134).
Analysis: Good access controls: (A) periodic reviews by process owners; (B) immediate disabling on exit; (C) role-based access avoiding SoD conflicts; (D) restricted, monitored admin accounts.
Distractors: (E) Shared accounts destroy traceability of who did what – nullifying the audit trail.

ICA-043.q: Match each application control with its objective:
ICA-043.e: Application controls are embedded in individual transactions.
p: Credit limit check on sales orders
ICA-043.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10–11 (ICR-137, ICR-165).
Analysis: Duplicate supplier invoice checks – prevent double payment; credit limit checks on sales orders – curb bad debt; batch totals – ensure complete processing; tax-code format checks – ensure accurate input.

ICA-044.q: An entity uses cloud (SaaS) accounting software. To assess the provider's controls, the entity/auditor usually relies on:
ICA-044.e: Users must still perform complementary controls such as internal access rights.
o: A service organisation controls report (SOC 1 Type 2 / ISAE 3402) plus complementary user entity controls (CUECs)
ICA-044.x:
Basis: VSA 402; ISAE 3402; AICPA SOC 1 (VSA-059, VSA-060, ICR-078).
Analysis: With SaaS accounting software, controls sit at the vendor → rely on a SOC 1 Type 2/ISAE 3402 report (design and operation over a period) and perform the complementary user entity controls (CUECs) it lists (internal access rights, access reviews).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't control evidence.

ICA-045.q: A SOC 1 Type 1 report assesses both design and operating effectiveness of controls over a period.
ICA-045.e: False. Type 1 covers design at a point in time; Type 2 also covers operating effectiveness over a period.
ICA-045.x:
Basis: VSA 402; ISAE 3402 (VSA-060).
Analysis: False. SOC 1 Type 1 covers the system description and suitability of control design at a point in time. Type 2 adds operating effectiveness over a period (usually 6–12 months) – needed when users or auditors want to rely on controls.

ICA-046.q: The most important payment-security control against business email compromise (BEC) changing supplier bank details is:
ICA-046.e: Contact details in a fake email are untrustworthy; use previously verified contacts.
o: Independent call-back via another channel (stored phone number in master data) before updating
Replying to the email to confirm
Asking the supplier to resend the email
ICA-046.x:
Basis: Internal control practice; ACFE; FBI IC3 (ICR-085, ICR-172).
Analysis: Fraudsters spoof supplier emails requesting account changes → all details in the email (phone numbers, contacts) may be fake. The key control: verify independently via a channel already in master data (call the number on file) before updating.
Distractors: B and D re-contact the fraudster; C – a test transfer only confirms the account exists, not who owns it.

ICA-047.q: Select ALL risks when using RPA (software bots) in accounts payable:
ICA-047.e: Automation changes rather than removes risk; govern bots like privileged users.
o: Bot logic changed outside change control
Mass repeated errors if input formats change
ICA-047.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11.
Analysis: RPA risks: (A) bots using over-privileged accounts – abuse, SoD conflicts; (B) bot logic changed outside change management; (C) mass repeated errors when input formats change – errors scale fast; (D) no accountable process owner.
Distractors: (E) Automation changes the form of risk; govern bots like privileged users (identity, access, logs, monitoring).

ICA-048.q: Arrange the standard program change management process:
ICA-048.e: Each step creates evidence for auditors to test.
o: Migration to production approved by someone independent of the developer
ICA-048.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (ICR-133).
Analysis: Order: change request logged and business-approved → development in a separate environment → user acceptance testing (UAT) → approval and promotion to production by someone independent of the developer → post-implementation review and records. Each step leaves evidence for ITGC testing.

ICA-049.e: An operating deficiency is when a well-designed control isn't performed properly.
o: A necessary control is missing, or exists but would not meet its objective even if operated as designed
A well-designed control is skipped by staff
A control is performed one day late
Two people sign instead of one
ICA-049.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; VSA 265.
Analysis: A design deficiency: a needed control is missing, or exists but wouldn't achieve its objective even if operated as designed (e.g., a review with no threshold or wrong focus). An operating deficiency: well designed but not performed, performed wrongly, or by someone lacking competence (B).
Distractors: C and D aren't the definition.

ICA-050.q: Match each deficiency level (VSA 265/ICFR) with its description:
ICA-050.e: VSA 265 requires written communication of significant deficiencies to those charged with governance.
p: Does not prevent/detect misstatements on a timely basis
Important enough to merit those charged with governance's attention
Reasonable possibility a material misstatement won't be prevented or detected timely
ICA-050.x:
Basis: VSA 265; COSO 2013; PCAOB AS 2201 (ICFR).
Analysis: A deficiency – a control fails to prevent, detect or correct misstatements in time; a significant deficiency (VSA 265) – important enough to merit governance's attention, communicated in writing (VSA-108); a material weakness – a reasonable possibility of material misstatement not being caught in time.

ICA-051.q: A daily control runs 250 times a year. The auditor samples 25 occurrences and finds 1 exception. What is the sample deviation rate (%)?
ICA-051.e: 1/25 = 4%; if zero deviations were planned, conclude the control is ineffective or extend the sample and investigate the cause.
ICA-051.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (audit sampling); VSA 330.
Working: Sample deviation rate = 1 / 25 = 4%.
Analysis: For a daily control, a sample of 25 usually assumes zero expected deviations. One exception → the projected population rate may exceed the tolerable rate → either don't rely on the control, or extend the sample and investigate the cause (isolated or systemic, intentional? – VSA 530 paras 12–13).
Check: 25 × 4% = 1 ✓.

ICA-052.q: Which test gives the strongest evidence of the operating effectiveness of a manual review control?
ICA-052.e: Inquiry alone is insufficient evidence of operating effectiveness.
o: Re-performance combined with inspection of documents
ICA-052.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 10; VSA 500 (audit procedures).
Analysis: Re-performance – the auditor independently redoing the control – combined with inspecting documents (review evidence, exceptions resolved) gives the strongest evidence of operating effectiveness because it directly verifies the outcome.
Distractors: B – inquiry alone isn't enough (VSA 330 para 10a requires combining it with other procedures); C – one observation only proves that moment, and people behave differently when watched; D – reading the procedure only shows design.

ICA-053.q: Assessing control design usually includes a walkthrough of one transaction from initiation to recording.
ICA-053.e: True. A walkthrough confirms understanding and that controls are implemented.
ICA-053.x:
Basis: VSA 315 (understanding IC, evaluating design and implementation).
Analysis: True. A walkthrough traces one transaction from initiation, approval, processing and recording to reporting, combining inquiry, observation and inspection → confirming the process is understood correctly and controls have been implemented.
Note: A walkthrough isn't enough to conclude on operating effectiveness over the period – tests of controls on a sample are needed (VSA 330).

ICA-054.e: Severity does not depend on the performer's seniority.
o: Potential misstatement magnitude (not just actual misstatements)
Whether compensating controls would prevent misstatement
ICA-054.x:
Basis: VSA 265 paras A6–A7; COSO 2013.
Analysis: Severity depends on: (A) the magnitude of potential misstatement, not just errors found; (B) whether compensating controls are precise enough to prevent or detect; (C) susceptibility of assets to misappropriation (cash, high-value stock); (D) multiple deficiencies affecting one account may combine into a significant one.
Distractors: (E) Seniority doesn't reduce the likelihood of error – long-trusted staff are often less supervised.

ICA-055.q: A factory manager's review of standard cost variances shows only a signature, no evidence of variance analysis. The auditor should:
ICA-055.e: A signature doesn't prove review precision; evidence of review content is needed.
o: Treat this as a precision risk; seek evidence of criteria and investigation, otherwise do not rely on the control
ICA-055.x:
Basis: VSA 330; practice for testing management review controls (ICA-024).
Analysis: A signature only proves 'signed', not that the review was precise enough. The auditor needs evidence of criteria and thresholds for investigating standard-cost variances, which variances were investigated, the findings and actions. Without it → the control isn't reliable → don't rely on it and expand substantive work on production cost.
Distractors: B accepts form over substance; C – more signature samples don't address precision; D – a material cycle can't be skipped.

ICA-056.q: Arrange the process for assessing internal control over a cycle (e.g., order-to-cash):
ICA-056.e: The risk and control matrix (RCM) links the steps.
o: Identify the cycle's objectives and misstatement risks
Flowchart and describe the process and key controls
Walkthrough to confirm design and implementation
Test operating effectiveness on a sample
ICA-056.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; VSA 315; VSA 330.
Analysis: Order: (1) define the cycle's objectives and misstatement risks (e.g., fictitious revenue, cut-off, uncollectible receivables); (2) flowchart and document the process and key controls; (3) walk through to confirm design and implementation (ICA-053); (4) test operating effectiveness on a sample; (5) evaluate deficiencies, report and remediate.
Note: A risk-control matrix (RCM) links risk → control → test → result across the steps.

ICA-057.q: An electronics component factory wants to assess the 'tone at the top'. The most suitable tool is:
ICA-057.e: Culture shows in actual behaviour and handling of breaches, not documents.
o: Anonymous ethics culture surveys and review of how past breaches were handled
ICA-057.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P1.
Analysis: Tone at the top shows in actual behaviour: how staff perceive leadership's attitude (anonymous surveys allow candour) and how past violations were handled (firmly and consistently, or excused for insiders – ICA-086).
Distractors: B – the number of documents doesn't reflect real culture; C and D are financial/operational data, not measures of ethical culture.

ICA-058.q: Risk assessment needs to be done only once when establishing the internal control system.
ICA-058.e: False. Risk assessment is iterative, especially when changes occur (P9).
ICA-058.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P7, P9.
Analysis: False. Risk assessment is iterative and ongoing: business, regulatory, technology and staffing conditions change → new risks emerge and existing ones shift. P9 requires identifying and assessing changes that could significantly affect IC (ICA-014) – e.g., a new ERP, market expansion, leadership change.

ICA-059.q: In the payroll cycle of a 2,000-worker manufacturer, which control best prevents 'ghost employees'?
ICA-059.e: Separate employee creation from payroll and reconcile to independent data.
o: HR (independent of payroll) maintains the employee master; payroll is periodically reconciled to biometric attendance and social insurance records
Payroll clerks create and delete employees
Cash wages paid via team leaders
Comparing total payroll with last year
ICA-059.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; ACFE – payroll fraud (ICR-090).
Analysis: 'Ghost employees' arise when one person can both create employee records and calculate and pay wages. The most effective controls: (1) segregation – an independent HR function owns the employee master, accounting only computes pay; (2) reconciliation to hard-to-fake independent data – biometric attendance and social insurance records.
Distractors: B concentrates rights; C – cash via team leaders is a classic risk channel; D – a total payroll comparison is too coarse to catch a few ghosts among 2,000 workers.

ICA-060.q: Select ALL suitable controls for cash at a retail store:
ICA-060.e: Voids need shift-manager approval and exception reporting.
o: Reconcile POS sales to cash deposited each shift
Letting cashiers void transactions without approval
ICA-060.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: Store cash controls: (A) reconcile POS sales to cash deposited each shift – detects shortages and assigns responsibility by shift; (B) surprise cash counts – deter and detect temporary 'borrowing'; (C) daily bank deposits – reduce cash on hand and theft risk; (D) cameras – monitoring and evidence.
Distractors: (E) Cashiers voiding transactions themselves is a common skimming technique (take cash, then void); voids need shift-manager approval and exception reporting.

ICA-061.q: After issuing an anti-bribery policy, the most effective communication is:
ICA-061.e: Communication must ensure recipients understand and can apply it in their work.
o: Scenario-based training per risk group (procurement, sales, projects), knowledge checks and sign-off
ICA-061.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P14 (internal communication).
Analysis: Effective communication must ensure recipients understand and can apply it. Scenario-based training for each high-risk group (purchasing – supplier gifts; sales – state customers; projects – permits), comprehension checks and signed compliance acknowledgements → evidence and accountability (P5).
Distractors: B, C and D are one-way messages with no check that recipients understood.

ICA-062.q: A well-run entity may reduce the frequency of separate evaluations if ongoing evaluations are effective and the environment is stable.
ICA-062.e: True. COSO allows a risk-based balance between ongoing and separate evaluations.
ICA-062.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P16.
Analysis: True. COSO allows a risk-based balance between ongoing and separate evaluations: if ongoing monitoring (dashboards, automated reconciliations, exception reviews) is effective and the environment stable, separate evaluations can be scaled back; with major changes or weak ongoing monitoring, increase them (ICA-033).

ICA-063.q: An automated invoice-to-PO price check (2% tolerance) works correctly, but 20 users can change the tolerance to 100%. Conclusion:
ICA-063.e: Application control reliance depends on ITGCs; configuration change logs are needed.
o: The application control can be undermined by an access ITGC deficiency; reassess and test configuration changes during the period
The control is effective since the logic was tested
ICA-063.x:
Basis: VSA 315; VSA 330 (application controls' dependence on ITGC).
Analysis: The 2% match logic works when tested, but 20 users can change the tolerance to 100% → the control could be switched off at any time (an access/configuration-change ITGC deficiency). Needed: reassess the deficiency, review configuration change logs over the whole period to see if tolerance was ever altered, and restrict rights.
Distractors: B – a test of one is valid only with effective ITGC (ICA-040); C and D ignore the risk.

ICA-064.q: A control deficiency over customer refunds: annual refunds total VND 1,200 million; an estimated 5% could be wrong/fraudulent undetected. What is the potential misstatement (VND million)?
ICA-064.e: 1,200 × 5% = 60 million; compare with materiality to assess severity.
ICA-064.x:
Basis: VSA 265 (evaluating deficiency severity); VSA 320 (materiality).
Working: Maximum potential misstatement = 1,200 × 5% = VND 60 million.
Analysis: Severity is judged on potential (possible) misstatement, not only errors found (ICA-054). Compare 60 million with performance and overall materiality, and consider nature – refunds are fraud-prone, so it may be qualitatively significant even if small.
Check: 60 / 1,200 = 5% ✓.

ICA-065.q: Consider these statements on the control environment:
ICA-065.e: Internal control provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
o: Job rotation in sensitive roles helps detect fraud.
A good control environment absolutely guarantees no fraud.
ICA-065.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (control environment; reasonable assurance limit).
Analysis: True – clear job descriptions define responsibility and authority (P3). True – job rotation and mandatory leave in sensitive roles expose frauds that need constant upkeep (e.g., lapping). False – IC gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance because of inherent limits (collusion, override – ICA-089). True – periodic competence reviews support P4.

ICA-066.q: A restaurant chain expands franchising into 3 new provinces in one year. The most prominent control risk under P9:
ICA-066.e: Rapid growth outpaces the control system.
o: Revenue, inventory and quality controls at new sites not uniformly deployed; new staff untrained
ICA-066.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P9 (identifying and analysing significant change).
Analysis: Franchising into 3 provinces in a year = fast growth, many new outlets and staff → revenue controls (POS, cash), ingredient stock, food quality and safety not rolled out consistently, staff untrained → leakage, errors, brand damage.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the most prominent risks for a domestically expanding restaurant chain.

ICA-067.q: Which control prevents selling beyond credit limits at a building materials distributor?
ICA-067.e: An automated preventive control with exception approval independent of sales.
o: ERP automatically blocks orders when balance + order exceeds the limit; exceptions approved by the CFO
AR clerk phones customers at month-end
ICA-067.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10–11 (automated preventive controls).
Analysis: Preventive control: the ERP automatically blocks orders when current balance + new order > credit limit; exceptions approved only by the CFO – independent of sales (who are incentivised by volume – ICA-007).
Distractors: B – collection calls are detective, after the sale; C – provisioning is an accounting consequence, not prevention; D – the year-end audit isn't the entity's control.

ICA-068.q: Manual journal entries in the general ledger need specific controls: approval by someone other than the preparer, supporting documents, and review of unusual entries (period-end, round sums, rarely used accounts).
ICA-068.e: True. They are the main channel for management override.
ICA-068.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; VSA 240 para 32 (testing journal entries).
Analysis: True. Manual journal entries in the general ledger are the main channel for management override and earnings adjustment. Controls: approval by someone other than the preparer; supporting documents; review of unusual entries – period-end, post-close, round amounts, rarely used accounts, unusual preparers. VSA 240 also requires auditors to test them.

ICA-069.q: Select ALL attributes to test in a sample of payment approvals:
ICA-069.e: Test attributes must link to the control objective.
ICA-069.x:
Basis: VSA 330; VSA 530 (test attributes).
Analysis: Attributes tied to payment-approval objectives: (A) the right authority under limits – prevents overreach; (B) approval before payment – after-the-fact approval loses preventive value (ICA-090); (C) complete documents – the three-way PO, receipt, invoice (ICA-026); (D) approver ≠ preparer – segregation.
Distractors: (E) Ink colour has nothing to do with the control objective.

ICA-070.q: An entity is hit by ransomware encrypting all accounting data. The control enabling the fastest recovery is:
ICA-070.e: Backups never restore-tested often fail when needed.
o: Regular segregated (offline/immutable) backups with periodic restore tests
ICA-070.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (8.13 information backup); COSO 2013 P11.
Analysis: Ransomware encrypts networked data, including permanently connected backups. Fast recovery needs isolated backups (offline, immutable) that don't get encrypted, and regular restore tests to prove backups work and meet RTO/RPO (ICR-105).
Distractors: B – antivirus is preventive, not recovery; C – changing passwords after the event doesn't restore data; D – more servers don't bring data back.

ICA-071.q: Under COSO, 'opportunity' is a fraud risk factor. Which example shows opportunity most clearly?
ICA-071.e: Pressure (debts, targets) and rationalisation (feeling underpaid) are the other fraud triangle elements.
o: The storekeeper also keeps records, with no independent counts
An employee has large personal debts
ICA-071.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P8; VSA 240 (fraud triangle).
Analysis: Opportunity = conditions allowing fraud to be committed and concealed, usually control gaps. A storekeeper who also keeps the ledger with no independent count can take goods and alter records (ICA-020) → the clearest opportunity.
Distractors: B – large personal debt and D – high targets are pressure/incentive; C – feeling underpaid is attitude/rationalisation.

ICA-072.q: Feedback from external auditors (management letters) and regulators is external information to be fed into internal control assessment.
ICA-072.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P15 (external communication).
Analysis: True. The external auditor's management letter (IC deficiencies found in the audit – VSA 265), tax or central-bank inspection findings, etc. are important outside inputs; management must receive, analyse and feed them into IC evaluation and remediation (P17).

ICA-073.q: The Audit Committee tracks remediation of control deficiencies most effectively through:
ICA-073.e: An issue log makes accountability and progress transparent.
o: An issue log with owners, deadlines, status and closure evidence
Asking the CEO verbally each quarter
ICA-073.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P17; IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 15.2).
Analysis: An issue log records the deficiency, severity, owner, due date, status and closure evidence (validated by IA – ICA-036) → the audit committee sees progress and overdue items and can hold people accountable.
Distractors: B – verbal updates have no evidence; C – the annual report lacks remediation detail; D – waiting a year leaves risk open too long.

ICA-074.q: Select ALL signs of a weak control environment:
ICA-074.e: Consistent two-level approvals are a positive sign.
o: Chief accountant replaced 3 times in 2 years
Unrealistic financial targets vs the market
Key decisions dominated by one person without effective oversight
ICA-074.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P1–5; VSA 240 (fraud risk factors).
Analysis: Signs of a weak control environment: (A) frequent chief-accountant turnover – possibly disputes with management over numbers, lost knowledge; (B) disdain for audit – poor tone at the top; (C) unrealistic targets – pressure for fraudulent reporting; (D) one-person dominance without oversight – override risk (P2).
Distractors: (E) Consistently operated two-level approval is a positive sign.

ICA-075.q: A real estate developer records apartment sales revenue. Which control matters most for 'occurrence' and 'cut-off'?
ICA-075.e: Property revenue is usually recognised on handover (transfer of control), not on deposit.
o: Matching recorded revenue to signed handover minutes and contractual payment schedules
ICA-075.x:
Basis: VAS 14 (sale-of-goods recognition criteria); IFRS 15 (transfer of control); VSA 315 (assertions).
Analysis: Apartment sales revenue is usually recognised on handover – when most risks and rewards/control pass to the buyer. Matching revenue to signed handover minutes (proof it occurred) and handover dates (cut-off), alongside contractual payment schedules.
Distractors: B and C – deposits and deposit contracts are customer advances, not revenue; D – advertising is irrelevant.

ICA-076.q: Periodic counts of fixed assets reconciled to the register are a safeguarding control activity.
ICA-076.e: True. They reveal lost, damaged or idle assets.
ICA-076.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: True. Periodic fixed-asset counts reconciled to asset cards and sub-ledgers are a detective safeguarding control: they reveal losses, damage, idle assets (needing disposal or impairment review) and assets present but unrecorded, and support the existence assertion.

ICA-077.q: A 'quarterly ERP access review' control is effective when:
ICA-077.e: The list must come from the system (complete, accurate) and reviewers must understand the business.
o: Process owners review system-generated user–role lists, record and fix inappropriate access
ICA-077.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (5.18 access rights).
Analysis: An access review is effective when: (1) the user–rights list is extracted directly from the system (complete and accurate – IPE, ICA-098); (2) the reviewer is the process owner who knows who needs what; (3) inappropriate rights are recorded and actually revoked or adjusted, with evidence.
Distractors: B – IT doesn't know business needs and reviews rights it granted; C – self-declared lists aren't reliable; D – it misses old accounts that accumulated rights.

ICA-078.q: For a weekly control (52 times/year), the auditor's sampling guide says 5–15 for weekly controls. If the lowest level is chosen, what is the sample size?
ICA-078.e: The usual minimum for weekly controls is 5, extended if risk is high.
ICA-078.x:
Basis: Audit practice on control test sample sizes by frequency; VSA 530.
Working: Weekly control (52/year), guidance 5–15 → minimum = 5.
Analysis: The low end applies when risk is low, no deviations are expected and the control is stable; move toward 15 for higher risk, heavier reliance or changes.
Note: Frequency-based sample tables are audit-firm practice, not figures prescribed in VSA.

ICA-079.q: A multinational's whistleblowing channel receives few reports although surveys show staff know of breaches. The most likely cause:
ICA-079.e: Needed: whistleblower protection, an independent third-party channel and feedback on outcomes.
o: Staff distrust anonymity and fear retaliation
ICA-079.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P14; ACFE Report to the Nations (ICR-101).
Analysis: Staff know of violations but don't report → the barrier is trust: fear of exposure, retaliation, or that nothing will happen. Fix: an independent (third-party) channel, guaranteed anonymity, anti-retaliation policy, feedback on outcomes (without revealing the reporter).
Distractors: B, C and D contradict the survey facts.

ICA-080.q: Consider these statements on internal control evaluation:
ICA-080.e: Severity is based on potential misstatement, not just actual errors.
o: A single deficiency may not be severe, but several combined may be a material weakness.
No actual misstatement found means no deficiency.
Compensating controls must be precise enough to reduce severity.
A material misstatement found by the auditor but not by controls is a strong indicator of weakness.
ICA-080.x:
Basis: VSA 265; COSO 2013; PCAOB AS 2201 (indicators of material weakness).
Analysis: True – several deficiencies affecting one account may combine into a material weakness. False – no actual misstatement doesn't mean no deficiency; severity is about potential misstatement (ICA-054). True – compensating controls must be precise enough to lower severity. True – a material misstatement found by the auditor but missed by controls strongly indicates a weakness.

ICA-081.q: In a conglomerate, an overseas subsidiary has a 'gift-giving' culture with state customers. The group should:
ICA-081.e: Corruption liability can extend to the parent (e.g., extraterritorial anti-bribery laws).
o: Apply a group-wide anti-bribery policy with threshold-based gift rules, registers and approvals, complying with local and extraterritorial laws
Let the subsidiary decide due to culture
Just book it as other expenses
ICA-081.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P1; ACFE; Anti-Corruption Law 2018 (non-state sector); extraterritorial anti-bribery laws (US FCPA, UK Bribery Act).
Analysis: Bribery risk at a subsidiary can expose the parent legally and reputationally. Fix: a group-wide anti-bribery policy – gift value thresholds, registration, prior approval, strict limits for officials; comply with local and extraterritorial laws; training and monitoring.
Distractors: B – 'local culture' doesn't remove legal liability; C is unrealistic; D hides the nature of the cost and increases risk.

ICA-082.q: A pharma company holds near-expiry stock. Controls that prevent losses and inventory misstatement:
ICA-082.e: FEFO and an independent destruction committee reduce fraud risk in write-offs.
o: Monthly batch/expiry ageing, FEFO process, committee-approved destruction with minutes
ICA-082.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; VAS 02 (inventories – net realisable value, write-downs).
Analysis: Control set: monthly ageing by batch and expiry (early action on near-expiry stock, write-downs under VAS 02); FEFO – first-expired, first-out, cutting expired stock; destruction through an independent committee with minutes – stops fake 'destruction' followed by resale.
Distractors: B – discretionary discounts create fraud opportunity; C – not recording misstates FS; D – a year-end count is too late.

ICA-083.q: Compliance risk (e.g., environmental or tax breaches) relates to one of COSO's objective categories, alongside operations and reporting.
ICA-083.e: True. COSO has three objective categories: operations, reporting and compliance.
ICA-083.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (the cube – three objective categories).
Analysis: True. COSO's three objective categories: operations (effectiveness, efficiency, safeguarding assets); reporting (financial and non-financial, internal and external); compliance (applicable laws and regulations – environment, tax, labour…). Environmental or tax violations are compliance risks.

ICA-084.q: Internal audit runs continuous analytics on 100% of payments. The main benefit versus sampling:
ICA-084.e: Analytics still need judgement on exceptions and don't replace first-line responsibility.
o: Earlier exception detection, full population coverage, investigation focused on risky items
Management controls are no longer needed
ICA-084.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024; COSO 2013 P16 (ICR-159).
Analysis: Continuous auditing on 100% of payments: full population coverage (no sampling risk), near-real-time detection of exceptions (duplicate payments, vendors sharing bank accounts with employees, off-hours transactions), and investigation focused on risky items.
Distractors: B – it doesn't replace first-line control responsibility; C – it can't eliminate fraud (collusion, formally valid transactions); D – judgement is still needed to set rules and handle exceptions.

ICA-085.e: Read-only report access does not create an execution–recording conflict.
o: Create sales orders and record cash receipts
Adjust inventory and hold physical stock
View revenue reports and view expense reports
ICA-085.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10–11; SoD conflict matrix (ICR-132).
Analysis: A conflict exists when one person both initiates/records and approves or holds assets: (A) create vendor + approve payment → fictitious vendors; (B) create sales orders + record receipts → cash theft hidden by writing down receivables; (C) adjust inventory + hold stock → take goods and adjust records; (D) create employees + run payroll → ghost employees (ICA-059).
Distractors: (E) Read-only report access doesn't allow executing or recording transactions.

ICA-086.q: After discovering the procurement head took kickbacks, management simply had him resign 'quietly' to protect reputation. The control consequence:
ICA-086.e: Consistent, transparent handling (within legal limits) sends an important deterrent message.
o: It weakens Principles 1 and 5: staff see breaches go unpunished, increasing rationalisation
No impact as the person left
ICA-086.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P1, P5; ACFE (fraud triangle – rationalisation).
Analysis: Letting a kickback-taker leave 'quietly' → staff see violations go unpunished and opaque → weakening P1 (ethics shown through actions) and P5 (accountability), and reinforcing rationalisation ('worst case I just resign'). The person may also reoffend elsewhere, and the entity loses the chance to recover losses.
Distractors: B, C and D misread the issue.

ICA-087.q: Which measure best reflects risk likelihood in quantitative assessment?
ICA-087.e: Combine historical data with judgement about future conditions.
o: Historical event frequency combined with forward-looking factors
Number of pages in the risk report
ICA-087.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (assessing risk severity); ISO 31000:2018.
Analysis: Likelihood is best quantified from historical event frequency (internal and industry loss data) combined with forward-looking factors (changing conditions, controls) – because the past doesn't always reflect the future.
Distractors: B – one person's feeling is subjective and biased; C and D – pages and meetings don't measure likelihood.

ICA-088.q: The cost of a control should not exceed its benefit (cost–benefit principle).
ICA-088.e: True. This is an inherent limitation of internal control.
ICA-088.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (inherent limitation – cost versus benefit).
Analysis: True. A control's benefits (losses avoided, information reliability) must justify its costs (staff, systems, process delay). E.g., two approvers aren't needed for VND 50,000 of stationery. This constraint is one reason IC gives only reasonable assurance (ICA-089).

ICA-089.q: Select ALL inherent limitations of internal control:
ICA-089.e: Because of these limitations, internal control provides only reasonable assurance.
ICA-089.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (inherent limitations of IC); VSA 315 paras A54–A56.
Analysis: Inherent limitations: (A) errors of judgement, fatigue, misunderstanding; (B) collusion defeating segregation; (C) management override (ICA-068); (D) cost-benefit constraints (ICA-088). Hence IC provides only reasonable assurance.
Distractors: (E) Expert-designed controls are a positive, not a limitation.

ICA-090.q: Internal audit finds 3 of 25 sampled purchase orders were approved after the invoice was received. Classification:
ICA-090.e: Severity also depends on transaction values and compensating controls.
o: Operating deficiency – the preventive control was performed late and lost its effect
Not a deficiency since signatures exist
ICA-090.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; VSA 265.
Analysis: The design requires approving POs before ordering (preventive) – sound design; but 3/25 samples (12%) were approved after the invoice arrived → late performance, losing preventive value → an operating deficiency (ICA-049).
Distractors: B – the design isn't flawed; C – a later signature doesn't substitute for prior approval; D – a material weakness can't be concluded yet; severity depends on transaction values and compensating controls (e.g., three-way match before payment).
Check: 3 / 25 = 12%.

ICA-091.q: At a logistics firm, per-vehicle fuel cost data come from fuel cards and GPS. A suitable information quality control:
ICA-091.e: Combining independent operational data helps detect fuel fraud.
o: Match litres consumed with GPS distance against standards, flag vehicles over standard
ICA-091.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P13 (quality information from independent sources).
Analysis: Matching litres consumed (fuel card) with GPS distance against each vehicle type's standard consumption → flag over-standard vehicles → investigate fuel fraud (fuelling other vehicles, resale, inflated mileage). Two data sources independent of drivers make the information reliable.
Distractors: B – driver-reported figures aren't independent; C – dropping GPS data loses the check; D – paying by advances doesn't control actual consumption.

ICA-092.q: Internal audit can design controls for a process and audit that same process the next year without affecting objectivity.
ICA-092.e: False. IIA standards require a cooling-off period or safeguards when assessing activities it previously designed or advised on.
ICA-092.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (Principle 2 – objectivity; standard 2.2 safeguarding objectivity).
Analysis: False. Auditing a process IA itself designed creates self-review – a bias toward rating one's own work well. IIA standards require a cooling-off period (typically at least 12 months for prior responsibility) or safeguards: assign other staff, independent review, disclose the limitation.
Note: Advising on control design is allowed if IA doesn't assume management responsibility.

ICA-093.q: An importer receives goods. A control over landed cost to avoid COGS and tax errors:
ICA-093.e: Landed cost includes purchase price, import duty, freight and insurance, all matched to documents.
o: Match customs declarations, commercial invoices, contracts and freight documents before costing receipts
ICA-093.x:
Basis: VAS 02 para 06 (inventory cost); COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: Imported stock cost = purchase price (commercial invoice, contract) + non-refundable import duty, special consumption and environmental taxes per the customs declaration + directly attributable freight, insurance and handling. Matching all documents before costing → accurate COGS consistent with taxes paid, and detection of declared-value gaps.
Distractors: B omits taxes and purchase costs; C – estimates misstate COGS; D – costing after sale misstates COGS of the period sold.

ICA-094.q: Select ALL measures that strengthen accountability (P5) for a retail chain's regional managers:
o: Balanced KPIs: sales, shrinkage, control compliance
Quarterly sub-certification of reports and controls
Internal audit results affect performance reviews
ICA-094.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P5 (enforcing accountability).
Analysis: Measures: (A) balanced KPIs covering sales, shrinkage and control compliance – avoiding sales-only drive (ICA-007); (B) quarterly sub-certifications on reports and controls – personal accountability; (C) clawback of bonuses when misconduct is found – reducing incentives to window-dress; (D) internal audit results feeding performance reviews.
Distractors: (E) Sales-only bonuses create pressure for distortion and fraud.

ICA-095.q: The auditor tests controls at mid-year (June) and finds them effective. For the remaining period (July–December), they should:
ICA-095.e: Roll-forward extent depends on risk, length of the remaining period and changes.
o: Obtain additional evidence for the remaining period (roll-forward), considering changes in controls and risk
ICA-095.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 12 (evidence obtained during an interim period).
Analysis: Interim control tests only prove effectiveness through June. For July–December a roll-forward is needed: obtain evidence on significant changes to controls after the interim period and decide what additional evidence the remaining period needs. Extent depends on misstatement risk, length of the remaining period, staff/system changes and reliance placed.
Distractors: B leaves half the year uncovered; C – retesting everything is excessive; D – inquiry alone isn't enough.

ICA-096.q: A company earns 60% of revenue from one customer. The risk and suitable response:
ICA-096.e: Concentration also affects going concern and credit risk assessments.
o: Customer concentration; diversify customers, long-term contracts, tight credit monitoring
ICA-096.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; VSA 570 (going concern – loss of a major customer is an indicator).
Analysis: 60% of revenue from one customer → concentration risk: losing the customer, price pressure or late payment could hit revenue, cash flow and even going concern. Responses: diversify customers, long-term contracts, tight credit monitoring (limits, guarantees, credit insurance).
Distractors: B and C aren't the risk the facts point to; D is wrong.

ICA-097.q: Arrange the process for handling an identified control deficiency:
ICA-097.e: Without root-cause analysis, issues tend to recur.
o: Agree remediation plan, owner and deadline
ICA-097.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P17; IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 15.2).
Analysis: Order: (1) record and assess severity (to prioritise and report at the right level); (2) analyse root cause (staffing, design, system, culture); (3) a remediation plan with owner and deadline; (4) implement; (5) retest effectiveness with independent evidence before closing (ICA-036).
Note: Skipping root-cause analysis tends to fix symptoms only, so the deficiency recurs.

ICA-098.q: System-generated reports (IPE – information produced by the entity) relied on by controls must be tested for completeness and accuracy.
ICA-098.e: True. A review control based on a wrong report is ineffective.
ICA-098.x:
Basis: VSA 500 para 9 (information produced by the entity); VSA 330.
Analysis: True. A review control relying on system reports (e.g., ageing or exception reports) is effective only if the report is complete and accurate. Testing IPE: reconcile totals to the ledger, check the query logic/parameters and related ITGC; if the report is wrong (missing rows, wrong ageing), the reviewer misses errors.

ICA-099.q: A construction company advances 30% of contract value to a subcontractor. Controls that reduce the risk of losing the advance:
ICA-099.e: Advance guarantees and deduction mechanisms are standard construction controls.
o: Require a bank advance-payment guarantee, recover advances pro rata to certified work, track advance ageing
ICA-099.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; Decree 37/2015/ND-CP (construction contracts – advance guarantees and recovery).
Analysis: Risk: a subcontractor takes a 30% advance and then fails to perform or goes bankrupt. Controls: a bank advance-payment guarantee (callable on default); recovering the advance progressively as a percentage of certified work on each payment; ageing advances to catch long-outstanding items.
Distractors: B relies on relationships, not controls; C – advancing more when behind schedule increases risk; D – no monitoring.
Note: Decree 37/2015 has been amended several times; check the current text when applying.

ICA-100.q: Management wants to state 'internal control over financial reporting is effective' in the annual report. The most appropriate basis:
ICA-100.e: An unmodified audit opinion on the FS doesn't mean internal control is effective.
o: A documented assessment against a recognised framework (COSO 2013), testing design and operation of key controls, evaluating deficiencies
ICA-100.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; SOX 404 (international practice on management's ICFR report).
Analysis: Stating 'ICFR is effective' needs a documented basis: an assessment against a recognised framework (COSO 2013), risk-based identification of key controls, testing design and operation, and evaluating deficiency severity (no material weakness at the assessment date).
Distractors: B – no misstatements found doesn't prove effective controls (ICA-080); C – an unmodified FS audit opinion is about the FS, not IC; D – a pledge isn't evidence.
